correctness.rationale: For each nontrivial tree component with v vertices and v-1 edge goods, no allocation can give every component vertex even one personally valued edge, and a vertex with zero own valued goods envies the recipient of some incident edge even if assigned outside component. Thus every such component forces at least one distinct envious agent. Orient each tree away from a root, and any cyclic component along one cycle then outward, assigning every good to its head: all other nonisolated vertices receive a valued good. In a SIMPLE graph any vertex values at most one edge in any other vertex's bundle, so every positive-own-good agent is nonenvious; exactly T(G) envious roots remain, with welfare |E|. For G(n,p), r isolated-edge components have exact factorial moment (n)_(2r)/2^r p^r(1-p)^(2r(n-r-1)); at p=(log n+loglog n+c)/(2n) this tends (e^-c/4)^r. Expected tree components of orders 3,4, middle sizes, and >n/2 all vanish using Cayley, a geometric bound and Chernoff, yielding Poisson(e^-c/4) for the minimum count. Independent exhaustive unrestricted edge-to-any-vertex allocations for all simple graphs n<=4 confirmed the deterministic optimum; not a proof of asymptotics.
residual_risks: Critical equality T(G) depends on a simple graph: multiple parallel valued goods can cause more than one valued item in another agent bundle.
Randomness is in G(n,p) and optimization is over complete allocations, not random allocation performance.
